notes.text: Deal gently — If you conquer (which be presaged they would by God's gracious answer to his prayer for the turning of Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness,) take him prisoner, but do not kill him. Which desire proceeded, from his great indulgence towards his children: from his consciousness that he himself was the meritorious cause of this rebellion, Absalom being given up to it for the punishment of David's sins; from the consideration of his youth, which commonly makes men foolish, and subject to ill counsels: and from his piety, being loth that he should be cut off in the act of his sin without any space for repentance. But "what means, says Bp. Hall, this ill-placed mercy? Deal gently with a traitor? Of all traitors with a son? And all this for thy sake, whose crown, whose blood he hunts after? Even in the holiest parents nature may be guilty of an injurious tenderness. But was not this done in type of that unmeasurable mercy, of the true King of Israel, who prayed for his murderers, Father, forgive them! Deal gently with them for my sake!" Yea, when God sends an affliction to correct his children, it is with this charge, deal gently with them for my sake: for he knows our frame.

The wood — More people died in the wood, either through hunger, and thirst, and weariness: or, by the wild beasts, whereof great numbers were there, which, though they were driven away from the place of the main battle, yet might easily meet with them when they fled several ways: or, by falling into ditches and pits, which were in that place, ver. 17, and probably were covered with grass or wood, so that they could not see them till they fell into them: and especially by David's men, who pursued them, and killed them in the wood: and the wood is rightly said to have devoured them, because it gave the occasion to their destruction, inasmuch as the trees, and ditches, and pits, entangled them, and stopped their flight, and made them an easy prey to David's men, who followed them, and slew them in the pursuit. The sword - In the main battle: the sword being put for the battle, by a common figure.

The servants of David — Who, according to David's command, spared him, and gave him an opportunity to escape. His head - In which probably he was entangled by the hair of the head, which being very long and thick, might easily catch hold of a bough, especially when the great God directed it. Either he wore no helmet, or he had thrown it away as well as his other arms, to hasten his flight. Thus the matter of his pride was the instrument of his ruin.

glossa.text: *And it happened that Absalom, sitting on a mule, met the servants of David.* ((RAB.)) Absalom, fleeing on a mule, was hanged in an oak by the hair of his head, etc., *as far as* they pass over into the dispersion of the nations, and they themselves lost the sovereignty and the people alike.

notes.text: Mark — Observe them accurately and punish them as they deserve. Stand - At thy tribunal.

Forgiveness — Thou art able and ready to forgive repenting sinners. Feared - Not with a slavish, but with a childlike fear. This mercy of thine is the foundation of all religion, without which men would desperately proceed in their impious courses.
I wait — That he would pardon my sins.
They — Whether soldiers that keep the night-watches in an army, or the priests or Levites who did so in the temple.

Israel — Every true Israelite. Plenteous - Abundantly sufficient for all persons who accept it upon God's terms. David testifies his humility, and exhorts Israel to trust in God, ver. 1-3. A song of degrees of David.

glossa.text:
*A canticle of degrees.* ((ID.)) The eleventh degree, etc., *as far as* a glad conclusion is set down with the certainty of pardon, there, *Let Israel hope in the Lord.*

*Out of the depths.* ((AUG.)) He who feels himself in the deep, etc., *as far as* as the Scripture says: *The sinner, when he shall have come into the depth of vices, contemneth.*

*Who shall abide it.* ((ID.)) Because well nigh all human life is barked at round about by sins, and every conscience is accused by its own thoughts. That heart is not chaste which presumes upon its own justice. Let it therefore presume upon the mercy of God, *For with him there is propitiation,* whence he subjoins:

*For with thee there is propitiation.* As it were: In what hope dost thou cry? Because there is mercy in thee, wherefore he speaks thus: Or join it thus.

((AUG.)) No man can abide it, etc., *as far as* one hope therefore there is: *For with thee there is propitiation,* etc., *For thy law's sake,* ((ID.)) I have waited for the *law* of mercy, etc., *as far as* and thou hast given this law in the very necessity.

*The morning.* ((ID.)) Let him hope in the morning watch who hopes for nothing else from God than immortality. *From the morning watch,* etc., *as far as* thence in the law the head and the tail of the victim were offered to the Lord. *Let Israel hope in the Lord.* ((CASS.)) The second part, where is the glad conclusion: Secure concerning himself, he preaches that they should hope always in the Lord. As it were, as his soul has hoped, so let Israel hope.
*And he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities.* ((ID.)) Here he has now said what that one shall do, whom he called merciful and plentiful.

notes.text: Wherefore — Seeing ye are thus created anew, walk accordingly, in every particular. For we are members one of another - To which intimate union all deceit is quite repugnant.

Be ye angry, and sin not — That is, if ye are angry, take heed ye sin not. Anger at sin is not evil; but we should feel only pity to the sinner. If we are angry at the person, as well as the fault, we sin. And how hardly do we avoid it. Let not the sun go down upon your wrath - Reprove your brother, and be reconciled immediately. Lose not one day. A clear, express command. Reader, do you keep it?
Neither give place to the devil — By any delay.

But rather let him labour — Lest idleness lead him to steal again. And whoever has sinned in any kind ought the more zealously to practice the opposite virtue. That he may have to give - And so be no longer a burden and nuisance, but a blessing, to his neighbours.

But that which is good — Profitable to the speaker and hearers. To the use of edifying - To forward them in repentance, faith, or holiness. That it may minister grace - Be a means of conveying more grace into their hearts. Hence we learn, what discourse is corrupt, as it were stinking in the nostrils of God; namely, all that is not profitable, not edifying, not apt to minister grace to the hearers.

Grieve not the Holy Spirit — By any disobedience. Particularly by corrupt discourse; or by any of the following sins. Do not force him to withdraw from you, as a friend does whom you grieve by unkind behaviour. The day of redemption - That is, the day of judgment, in which our redemption will be completed.

Let all bitterness — The height of settled anger, opposite to kindness, ver. 32. And wrath - Lasting displeasure toward the ignorant, and them that are out of the way, opposite to tenderheartedness. And anger - The very first risings of disgust at those that injure you, opposite to forgiving one another. And clamour - Or bawling. "I am not angry," says one; "but it is my way to speak so." Then unlearn that way: it is the way to hell. And evil speaking - Be it in ever so mild and soft a tone, or with ever such professions of kindness. Here is a beautiful retrogradation, beginning with the highest, and descending to the lowest, degree of the want of love.
As God, showing himself kind and tenderhearted in the highest degree, hath forgiven you.
Be ye therefore followers — Imitators. Of God - In forgiving and loving. O how much more honourable and more happy, to be an imitator of God, than of Homer, Virgil, or Alexander the Great!

glossa.text: *For which cause.* He follows out the parts of the old and of the new man. *With his neighbour.* Even with a Gentile: because every man is a neighbour by the condition of the first birth, or by the hope of conversion every man ought to be thought a neighbour.

*Be ye angry,* that is, be indignant with your own selves with such vehemence that you cease from sinning, because upon this anger the sun of justice does not go down, but rather shines upon it. Anger is a natural motion of the mind against sinners; but lest by exceeding the measure you sin by reproving too harshly. Whence Solomon: *Be not too just, who perisheth by his own justice ((Eccl. VII))* . Justice therefore must be tempered, whence God also bears with the wicked, that some of them may be corrected. *Let not the sun go down.* He wills that anger endure not, because if it endures, occasion is given to the devil. For the angry man thinks evil, and so the devil insinuates himself that he may accomplish evils. *Let not the sun go down.* Let not Christ forsake the mind, who never dwells with anger.

*Do not,* etc. There are two gates by which the devil enters: cupidity and fear concerning earthly things. These same being turned to the contrary, God enters. Those are to be shut, these to be opened.
*Every word,* etc. In the servant of God all things ought to be seen to be good, nor ought his purity to be stained in any part.

*And grieve not.* Through disobedience, *the Holy Spirit,* that is, the preacher of the truth, which is to grieve the Holy Spirit so far as pertains to you. Which you ought not to do, in whom you have been sealed as wax, his image being left with you; or you have been sealed, that is, set apart from the wicked.

*All bitterness.* These things, even if they be done when causes arise, must nevertheless be tempered. *Blasphemy.* Blasphemy is that by which false things are said concerning God himself. And therefore it is worse to blaspheme than to forswear, because by forswearing God is brought in as witness to a false thing; but by blaspheming false things are said concerning God himself.

*Unto an odour of sweetness.* If the death of Christ was a sweet odour to God, therefore he willingly accepted his death. Did not they, then, sin who crucified him? But it is not so, because they unjustly slew the just one: who was offered by the Father's will and by his own. So also Judas, what has he but sin in betraying Christ? yet unless Christ had delivered up himself, Judas would not have delivered him up. Judas delivered up Christ, Christ delivered up himself. But the one was transacting the business of his own selling, the other of our redemption. Therefore the one impiously offended, this one acted mercifully.

notes.text: I am the bread of life — Having and giving life: he that cometh -he that believeth - Equivalent expressions: shall never hunger, thirst - Shall be satisfied, happy, forever.

echoes.text: Come to me, you that are desirous of me, And be you filled with my produce. For my memorial is sweeter than honey, And my inheritance than the honeycomb. They that eat me will yet be hungry; And those who drink me will yet be thirsty.
echoes.note: Wisdom says 'Come to me... those who eat me will hunger for more, those who drink me will thirst for more.' John inverts it ('will never hunger... never thirst'), a deliberate transformation signalling Jesus surpasses Wisdom/Torah. High Availability and Coherence; the inversion is the point.

echoes.text: They shall not hunger nor thirst; neither shall the heat nor sun strike them: for he who has mercy on them will lead them, even by springs of water he will guide them.
echoes.note: 'They shall not hunger or thirst... he who has pity will lead them' supplies the hunger-and-thirst-abolished promise of the eschatological return. Coheres tightly with v.35's double negation; an exilic-restoration backdrop to the bread of life.

echoes.text: Many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
echoes.note: The repeated 'I will raise him up at the last day' (vv.39-40) draws on the clearest OT resurrection text, 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake... to everlasting life.' Provides the Availability for John's last-day raising; recurs across the discourse.

notes.text: Into the wilderness — The vast wilderness of Arabia. He durst not stay in Judah, tho' good Jehosaphat reigned there, because he was allied to Ahab, and was a man of an easy temper, whom Ahab might circumvent, and either by force or art seize upon Elijah. It is enough - I have lived long enough for thy service, and am not like to do thee any more service; neither my words nor works are like to do any good upon these unstable and incorrigible people. I am not better - That I should continue in life, when other prophets who have gone before me, have lost their lives.

Angel of the Lord, &c. — He needed not to complain of the unkindness of men, when it was thus made up by the ministration of angels. Wherever God's children are, they are still under their father's eye.

And went — He wandered hither and thither for forty days, 'till at last he came to Horeb, which in the direct road was not above three or four days journey. Thither the spirit of the Lord led him, probably beyond his own intention, that he might have communion with God, in the same place that Moses had.

glossa.text: *And behold an angel of the Lord touched him.* ((RAB.)) The angel who fed Elias signifies the angel of great counsel; by whose work we subsist both in bodily and in spiritual nature.

*And behold at his head,* etc. ((ID.)) Elias twice fed expresses the infirmity of our nature, for whom a single feeding does not suffice, but a double, that we may be able to ascend to things above. For as the body cannot subsist without bodily food, so neither can the soul live without the word of God.

((ID.)) So we also, when we shake off from us the sleep of sloth, must needs, being strengthened by divine comfort, hasten with all our might, by the step of good works, through all the time of the present life, to ascend into the mountain of God and into his holy place, that there we may find eternal rest.

notes.text: Shall boast — Shall glory in this, that I have so powerful and so gracious a master. The humble - The righteous.
Together — Not in place, for David was now banished from the place of God's publick worship, but in affection: let our souls meet, and let our praises meet in the ears of the all-hearing God.
Lightened — Comforted and encouraged. Ashamed - They were not disappointed of their hope.
This man — David.
The angel — The angels, the singular number being put for the plural.
O taste — Make trial, of it by your own experience of it. Good - Merciful and gracious.

glossa.text: *I will bless.* ((CASS.)) The second psalm through an imperfect alphabet, etc., *as far as* he is glorified together with him.

*In the Lord shall my soul be praised.* ((ID.)) For his own praise is the preaching of his Lord, as a good servant glories in the good repute of his lord. *The meek.* Not the learned, not those who fast, because they are proud: but the meek, because they have temperance in all things. The meek, not being proud of their own understanding; not bearing the yoke of God after the manner of the untamed.

*O magnify the Lord.* Spiritual grace does not wish to do alone what profits many; whence it calls others: *Magnify,* that it might draw those invited, it tells what goods came to it thereby: *I sought the Lord. Out of all.* It cannot be told piecemeal how great things he obtained who sought nothing other than God. *Come ye.* ((CASS.)) Now piecemeal he admonishes the saints concerning the new countenance. As if to say, *Magnify:* and if among the first, come ye into what is pleasant. Or, *Magnify,* and in what order? behold: *Come ye* by faith. ((AUG.)) Come ye by cleaving with faith, and by running with the two feet of a twin charity. ((CASS.)) The praises being set first, he exhorts to communion. *Let them not be confounded.* ((AUG.)) Whatever happens here to the just man, he does not blush, because he is always the higher with God: but the proud man blushes in adversities, because he has not drawn near to God.

*The poor man.* ((CASS.)) *This one* is here the spiritual man, because he draws near and is enlightened, and shall not blush; because, when he cries out, he is freed from all the straits of the world at his death, when he now passes over to God.

*He shall send in an Angel. Come ye,* and as this poor man cried out and was heard, in the same way *he shall send in an Angel,* etc. ((AUG.)) *He shall send in an Angel.* Other interpreters have rendered it thus: *The Angel of the Lord surroundeth in a ring them that fear him.* An Angel from heaven, or a man, who is a minister of the will of God. Faulty codices have it. *The Lord shall send in an Angel.*

*Taste and see.* Here openly of the sacrament which he bore in his hands. *Taste* the flesh and blood of Christ. *The Lord is sweet.* ((ID.)) And delightful: because he is life to him that takes him, driving away all troubles in the world to come, that is: Hope through this for eternal life. ((CASS.)) And because God is life, the flesh which he united to himself is life-giving.

notes.text: Wherefore — Seeing ye are thus created anew, walk accordingly, in every particular. For we are members one of another - To which intimate union all deceit is quite repugnant.

Be ye angry, and sin not — That is, if ye are angry, take heed ye sin not. Anger at sin is not evil; but we should feel only pity to the sinner. If we are angry at the person, as well as the fault, we sin. And how hardly do we avoid it. Let not the sun go down upon your wrath - Reprove your brother, and be reconciled immediately. Lose not one day. A clear, express command. Reader, do you keep it?
Neither give place to the devil — By any delay.

But rather let him labour — Lest idleness lead him to steal again. And whoever has sinned in any kind ought the more zealously to practice the opposite virtue. That he may have to give - And so be no longer a burden and nuisance, but a blessing, to his neighbours.

But that which is good — Profitable to the speaker and hearers. To the use of edifying - To forward them in repentance, faith, or holiness. That it may minister grace - Be a means of conveying more grace into their hearts. Hence we learn, what discourse is corrupt, as it were stinking in the nostrils of God; namely, all that is not profitable, not edifying, not apt to minister grace to the hearers.

Grieve not the Holy Spirit — By any disobedience. Particularly by corrupt discourse; or by any of the following sins. Do not force him to withdraw from you, as a friend does whom you grieve by unkind behaviour. The day of redemption - That is, the day of judgment, in which our redemption will be completed.

Let all bitterness — The height of settled anger, opposite to kindness, ver. 32. And wrath - Lasting displeasure toward the ignorant, and them that are out of the way, opposite to tenderheartedness. And anger - The very first risings of disgust at those that injure you, opposite to forgiving one another. And clamour - Or bawling. "I am not angry," says one; "but it is my way to speak so." Then unlearn that way: it is the way to hell. And evil speaking - Be it in ever so mild and soft a tone, or with ever such professions of kindness. Here is a beautiful retrogradation, beginning with the highest, and descending to the lowest, degree of the want of love.
As God, showing himself kind and tenderhearted in the highest degree, hath forgiven you.
Be ye therefore followers — Imitators. Of God - In forgiving and loving. O how much more honourable and more happy, to be an imitator of God, than of Homer, Virgil, or Alexander the Great!

glossa.text: *For which cause.* He follows out the parts of the old and of the new man. *With his neighbour.* Even with a Gentile: because every man is a neighbour by the condition of the first birth, or by the hope of conversion every man ought to be thought a neighbour.

*Be ye angry,* that is, be indignant with your own selves with such vehemence that you cease from sinning, because upon this anger the sun of justice does not go down, but rather shines upon it. Anger is a natural motion of the mind against sinners; but lest by exceeding the measure you sin by reproving too harshly. Whence Solomon: *Be not too just, who perisheth by his own justice ((Eccl. VII))* . Justice therefore must be tempered, whence God also bears with the wicked, that some of them may be corrected. *Let not the sun go down.* He wills that anger endure not, because if it endures, occasion is given to the devil. For the angry man thinks evil, and so the devil insinuates himself that he may accomplish evils. *Let not the sun go down.* Let not Christ forsake the mind, who never dwells with anger.

*Do not,* etc. There are two gates by which the devil enters: cupidity and fear concerning earthly things. These same being turned to the contrary, God enters. Those are to be shut, these to be opened.
*Every word,* etc. In the servant of God all things ought to be seen to be good, nor ought his purity to be stained in any part.

*And grieve not.* Through disobedience, *the Holy Spirit,* that is, the preacher of the truth, which is to grieve the Holy Spirit so far as pertains to you. Which you ought not to do, in whom you have been sealed as wax, his image being left with you; or you have been sealed, that is, set apart from the wicked.

*All bitterness.* These things, even if they be done when causes arise, must nevertheless be tempered. *Blasphemy.* Blasphemy is that by which false things are said concerning God himself. And therefore it is worse to blaspheme than to forswear, because by forswearing God is brought in as witness to a false thing; but by blaspheming false things are said concerning God himself.

*Unto an odour of sweetness.* If the death of Christ was a sweet odour to God, therefore he willingly accepted his death. Did not they, then, sin who crucified him? But it is not so, because they unjustly slew the just one: who was offered by the Father's will and by his own. So also Judas, what has he but sin in betraying Christ? yet unless Christ had delivered up himself, Judas would not have delivered him up. Judas delivered up Christ, Christ delivered up himself. But the one was transacting the business of his own selling, the other of our redemption. Therefore the one impiously offended, this one acted mercifully.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The crowd grumbled: is this not Joseph's son?
Yet the Father draws us, and we come.
I am the living bread come down from heaven.
Whoever eats this bread will live forever.
Out of the depths we wait for the Lord.
More than the watchman waits for morning.
Come, you who hunger for life; come, let us worship.
We come to the living bread. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: They grumble among themselves: we know his father and mother, so who is he to come down from heaven?
Give us this bread always.
No one comes unless the Father draws them, and you are here, which means you have already been drawn by a love older than your doubt.
Give us this bread always.
I am the living bread, he says; eat this bread and you will live forever, for the bread I give is my own flesh for the life of the world.
Give us this bread always.
So come up out of the depths, all you who wait for morning; the bread of heaven is set before you now.
Give us this bread always.
